course.title: Construction: How a House Is Built
course.lead: A free, self-paced course on how a house goes together, from the soil and foundation up through the frame, roof and walls to the finishes: what each part does, the physics that holds it up and keeps it dry, how to spot trouble, what you can safely do yourself, and when to call a licensed pro or an engineer.
course.who: Written for teens and adults with no building experience. It picks up where the home guides in Being an Adult 101 leave off.
course.why: Each lesson explains the “why” as well as the “what”: how loads flow to the ground, why a deeper joist is so much stiffer, why concrete hardens without drying, how heat and water vapor move through a wall. Facts and numbers come from U.S. government agencies (OSHA, EPA, the Department of Energy and ENERGY STAR, the Forest Products Laboratory, the Bureau of Labor Statistics), university extension and engineering programs, and OpenStax textbooks, and every lesson lists its sources.
how: Start with Lesson 1 for the big picture, then go in order or jump to the part of the house you’re curious about.
Each lesson has labeled diagrams, a “parts and what they do” table, a short quiz and links to go deeper. Badges show the level.
Play with the interactive pieces: the load path, the sagging joist, the wall you frame yourself, the wall that handles rain and vapor, and more.
Use the troubleshooting finder when something seems wrong, and climb the skill ladder one rung at a time.
course.final: The local code is the final word. This course explains how houses are built in general. The building code your city or county has adopted, and the building department that enforces it, decide what’s required where you live, including which work needs a permit and inspections. Structural changes need a permit and often an engineer, and some work legally needs a licensed contractor. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions for every product.

lessons.title: The Big Picture
lessons.short: How a house goes up, in order; who does each part; and why codes, permits and inspections exist.
lessons.intro: A house is built from the ground up, in an order that lets each crew work on what the last one finished. This lesson walks through that order, meets the people who do each part, and explains the rules that keep the result safe. The map shows every system in one house.

blocks.html:
Every wood-frame house follows roughly the same path from bare ground to move-in day.

  1. Site work. The lot is cleared, the hole for the foundation is dug, and the ground is shaped so rain will drain away from the house later. Lesson 3
  2. Foundation. Concrete footings spread the house’s weight over the soil. Walls or a slab go on top. Lesson 3
  3. Framing. Carpenters build the floors, walls and roof frame, the skeleton of the house. Lesson 4
  4. Roof, windows and doors. Once the roof is covered and the windows and outside doors are in, the house is “dried in”: rain stays out, and the inside work can begin. Lesson 5
  5. Rough-ins. Plumbers, electricians and HVAC technicians run pipes, wires and ducts through the open walls, floors and ceilings.
  6. Insulation and air sealing. The walls and attic are insulated, and gaps are sealed. Lesson 6
  7. Drywall. Sheets of gypsum board cover the framing, and the joints are taped and smoothed. Lesson 7
  8. Finishes. Trim, doors, floors, paint, cabinets, light fixtures and faucets go in last.

blocks.h: The rough-ins: where the other trades come in
blocks.html:
“Rough-in” is the stage when pipes, wires and ducts are run through the open framing, before insulation and drywall cover them. Three other trades do this work, and each has its own course in The Trades:

  • Plumbing: water supply lines, and the drain and vent pipes that carry wastewater away. The Trades: Plumbing
  • Electrical: the service panel, cables, and the boxes for outlets, switches and lights. The Trades: Electrical
  • HVAC: the furnace, air conditioner or heat pump, and the ducts that carry air to each room. The Trades: HVAC

Inspectors check plumbing, electrical and other systems to make sure they meet the code. Rough-in work usually gets inspected while the walls are still open.
A house takes many trades. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics describes each one in its Occupational Outlook Handbook:

blocks.html:
A building code is a set of minimum rules for building safely: how strong the structure must be, how the house resists fire, how stairs are built, how much insulation it needs, and much more. Many states and cities base their rules on model codes, such as the International Residential Code for houses and the International Energy Conservation Code for energy use, and they may change them. The building department where you live decides which rules apply there. Builders call it the authority having jurisdiction.

Before most building work starts, the builder or owner applies for a permit. A plans examiner checks the drawings against the adopted codes. Then building inspectors visit the job several times: an early check, follow-up inspections as the work goes on, and a full examination when it’s done. Inspectors can issue violation notices and stop-work orders if the work doesn’t comply.

A home inspector is different. A buyer usually hires one to report on a house’s structure and condition, but home inspectors have no authority to enforce the building code.

lessons.title: Loads and Structure
lessons.short: Dead, live, snow and wind loads; the load path from roof to soil; why triangles are stiff and deep beams sag less.
lessons.intro: Every pound in a house, from the shingles to the people in the kitchen, has to find its way down to the ground. Builders call that route the load path. This lesson follows it, names the four ways a part can be loaded, and shows why a deeper joist is so much stiffer.

blocks.html:
A house carries several kinds of load at once:

  • Dead load is the weight of the building itself: framing, sheathing, drywall, roofing, flooring.
  • Live load is everything that moves or changes: people, furniture, appliances, stored things.
  • Snow load is the weight of snow on the roof, which can be large in snowy places.
  • Wind load pushes on walls and the roof. At the roof’s edges, wind creates both the biggest pushes and the biggest pulls, so a roof has to be held down as well as held up.

Designers plan for the loads the local code sets for their area. A house in snow country carries a bigger roof load than one on the Gulf Coast, and a house near the coast plans for stronger winds.

Follow a pound of snow. It presses on the roof sheathing, which rests on the trusses or rafters. They sit on the top plates of the walls. The studs carry it down to the bottom plate, through the floor’s rim joist, sill plate and foundation wall, into the footing, and finally into the soil. Inside the house, floor joists hand part of their load to a beam, the beam rests on posts, and each post stands on its own footing.

Every link in that chain has to carry its share, and so does every connection between links: nails, plates, bolts and straps. The foundation is tied to the framing with anchor bolts or straps at the sill plate.

Physics sees each piece as an object in equilibrium. Nothing in a sound house is speeding up, so the forces on every piece add to zero: the load pushing down on a stud is matched by the plate pushing up. In the end the soil pushes up on the footings exactly as hard as the house pushes down, which is Newton’s third law at work.

blocks.cap: Drag the sliders to add snow and furniture, change the footing width, or open a window in the wall. Only the loads you add are counted; the house’s own weight would add more. Pressure = force ÷ area.

blocks.html: pressure on the soil = load on the footing ÷ footing area  <small>(P = F / A)</small>

A part can be loaded four basic ways. Compression squeezes it shorter, like a post or a stud. Tension stretches it longer, like the bottom chord of a roof truss that keeps the walls from spreading. Bending does both at once: a loaded joist is squeezed along its top edge and stretched along its bottom edge. Shear is a sideways force that makes one layer try to slide past another, as at a bolted joint.

Materials handle these differently. Concrete can withstand compression well, which is why it works for footings and columns, but its tensile strength is only about 10 to 15 percent of its compressive strength. That’s why concrete is almost always reinforced with steel, which takes the tension (Lesson 3).

blocks.html:
Nail four boards into a rectangle and push on a corner: the frame racks over into a parallelogram, because nothing about four side lengths fixes the angles. Three boards in a triangle can’t do that. Three side lengths fix all three angles, so the only way to change the triangle’s shape is to stretch or squeeze one of its sides. The push turns into tension and compression in the members, which wood handles well.

That’s the idea behind a roof truss, a frame built entirely of triangles. Walls use the same trick another way: wood sheathing panels nailed to the studs make the wall act like one stiff sheet that can’t rack. Walls built to resist sideways forces from wind this way are called shear walls.

blocks.h: Beams, and why depth matters so much
blocks.html: A joist, rafter, header or beam works in bending. How much it sags depends on four things: the load, the span, the stiffness of the material (its modulus of elasticity, E), and the shape of its cross-section (its moment of inertia, I). For a beam resting on two supports with the load spread evenly along it, the sag at the middle is:

sag = 5 × w × L⁴ ÷ (384 × E × I)  where w = load per inch of length, L = span
I = b × h³ ÷ 12  for a rectangle b wide and h deep

blocks.h: Depth cubed, span to the fourth
blocks.html: Two exponents explain a lot about houses. Depth is cubed in the stiffness, so a board twice as deep is eight times as stiff. That’s why joists stand on edge, and why a 2×4 laid flat bends like a diving board. Span is raised to the fourth power in the sag, so doubling the span of a joist under the same load per foot makes it sag sixteen times as much. Wood species matters too: in the USDA Wood Handbook’s tables, measured at 12 percent moisture, Douglas-fir’s E is about 1.95 million pounds per square inch and ponderosa pine’s about 1.29 million.

blocks.cap: Pick a size, stand it on edge or lay it flat, and change the span and the load. The sag is drawn bigger than life so you can see it; the number is the real one. The joist’s own weight, knots, long-term creep and code limits are left out.

blocks.h: Never cut, notch or remove structure without a plan
blocks.html: Load-bearing walls, beams, joists, headers, posts and truss members are links in the load path. Removing a wall, cutting a joist for a pipe, or notching a beam can overload the parts left behind. These changes need a permit and, often, an engineer’s design. Real joist and beam sizes come from the span tables in the local code or from an engineer, not from a calculator like this one.

quiz.q: Furniture and people in a house are what kind of load?
quiz.why: Live loads move or change. The weight of the building itself is dead load.

quiz.q: What carries the load over a window opening to the studs on each side?
quiz.why: The header is a short beam that carries the load sideways to the jack studs.

quiz.q: A 2×12 (11¼ inches deep) is about twice as deep as a 2×6 (5½ inches). Under the same load and span, how does its sag compare?
quiz.why: Stiffness grows with depth cubed: 2.05³ ≈ 8.6, so the 2×12 sags about 8.6 times less.

quiz.q: Why is concrete reinforced with steel?
quiz.why: Concrete’s tensile strength is only about 10 to 15 percent of its compressive strength, so steel carries the tension.

quiz.q: If you make a footing twice as wide and the load stays the same, the pressure on the soil…
quiz.why: Pressure is force divided by area. Twice the area, half the pressure.

lessons.title: Site and Foundations
lessons.short: Soil and drainage, footings below the frost line, slabs, crawlspaces and basements, concrete and rebar, and keeping water out.
lessons.intro: A foundation has two jobs. It spreads the weight of the house over enough soil to hold it, and it keeps the wood frame up out of the wet ground. Both start with the site: the soil and, above all, where the water goes.

blocks.h: Start with the site: soil and water
blocks.html:
Water is a foundation’s main enemy, and a roof collects a lot of it. In a 1-inch rain, about 1,250 gallons of water fall on the roof of a 2,000-square-foot house. All of it has to go somewhere other than the basement.

So the ground around a house is shaped to slope away from it. Sources give slightly different minimums: University of Minnesota Extension suggests at least 1 inch per foot for at least 6 feet, and the Department of Energy’s building science guidance calls for at least half an inch per foot for 10 feet. Your local code sets the rule where you live. Gutters and downspouts carry roof water away too: Minnesota Extension suggests at least one downspout for every 50 feet of eave, with extensions that discharge the water at least 4 feet from the wall.

Soil also matters. Water can climb up through soil by capillary action, the way it climbs a paper towel. In gravel it rises only a few inches; in sand, 1 to 8 feet; in silt, 12 to 16 feet; and in clay, 12 to 20 feet.

Before anyone digs, the buried utilities have to be located. OSHA’s first rule for preventing electrocution on a job site is to locate and identify utilities before starting work.

A footing is a wide strip or pad of concrete under a wall or post. Since pressure is force divided by area, a wider footing spreads the same load over more soil, so the soil is pressed less.

In cold climates, footings are set deeper than the ground freezes. Water expands as it freezes (ice has a more open crystal structure, which is why it floats), so wet soil that freezes can swell and lift whatever sits on it. That’s called frost heave. The local building department sets how deep footings must go where you live.

blocks.html:
• Slab-on-grade: a concrete floor poured right on the ground, usually with thickened edges or separate footings around the outside. Under the slab goes a capillary break: a layer of gravel, sand or crushed stone about 4 inches thick, covered with polyethylene sheeting at least 6 mil thick, overlapped 6 to 12 inches and sealed at the seams. It keeps ground moisture from wicking up into the concrete.
  • Crawlspace: short foundation walls lift the floor framing off the ground, leaving a low space underneath. The soil inside is covered with polyethylene at least 6 mil thick, sealed at the seams and run at least 6 inches up the walls and piers, whether the crawlspace is vented or not. Without it, moisture from the soil can lead to mold and rot on the joists.
  • Basement: full-height foundation walls with a slab floor. The outside of the walls below ground is damp-proofed, the backfill is gravel so water can drain down, and a perforated drain pipe at the footing carries the water away.

blocks.h: Concrete hardens by hydration, not by drying
blocks.html:
Concrete is a mix of portland cement, water and aggregates (sand and gravel or crushed stone), and the aggregate makes up roughly 70 to 80 percent of its volume. The cement and water form a paste that binds the aggregate together.

Here’s the surprising part: concrete doesn’t harden by drying out. It hardens through a chemical reaction between the cement and the water, called hydration. As long as water is present, hydration keeps going, for years. Concrete that is allowed to dry in air gains only about half the strength of concrete kept continuously moist.

That’s why fresh concrete is cured: kept moist and warm while it gains strength. The first 7 to 10 days are critical; the concrete shouldn’t freeze or dry out. Builders keep it wet by ponding, spraying or fogging, or wet coverings, or seal the water in with plastic sheeting, curing compounds, or by leaving the forms in place. About 90 percent of its strength comes in the first 28 days, so 28-day strength is the standard reference. Most structural concrete reaches 3,000 to 5,000 psi in compression.

The mix matters too. The ratio of water to cement is the single most important factor in strength: less water makes stronger concrete. About 0.3 is the minimum needed for full hydration, and practical mixes run about 0.4 to 0.6. Too much water makes weak concrete; too little makes it unworkable.
water–cement ratio = water ÷ cement  <small>lower ratio → stronger concrete (practical range about 0.4 to 0.6)</small>

Concrete is strong when squeezed but weak when stretched: its tensile strength is only about 10 to 15 percent of its compressive strength. So it’s almost never used without reinforcement. Steel reinforcing bars, or rebar, carry the tension and limit how wide cracks can open.

Concrete also shrinks as it loses water, and that shrinking creates tension inside it. That’s one reason concrete and concrete-block foundations usually develop some cracks, and why a hairline crack is not automatically a problem (Lesson 11).

blocks.h: Keeping water and soil gas out
blocks.html:
Gutters, downspout extensions, grading, damp-proofing and drain tile all work to keep outside water away from the foundation. A sump pump is a backup that can fail, and its pit should have an airtight, childproof cover. A dehumidifier helps with dampness and odor but doesn’t fix the cause.

Soil gas matters too. Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive gas, made by the decay of uranium in soil and water. You can’t see it or smell it, and it can enter homes from the ground and build up to dangerous levels. EPA says radon exposure is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking, that testing is the only way to know your level, and that all homes should be tested.

• Keep gutters clean, and extend downspouts so water lands well away from the house.
  • Keep soil and mulch sloping away from the foundation.
  • Test your home for radon with a test kit, as EPA recommends.
  • Learn where your main water shutoff is (Being an Adult 101).

blocks.h: Stop: foundations and trenches are for pros
blocks.html:
Foundation repairs, underpinning and anything that changes how the house is supported need a permit and a structural engineer or experienced foundation contractor. If a crack keeps growing, or a wall bows or leans, have it looked at.

Digging is dangerous too. OSHA says never to enter an unprotected trench or excavation 5 feet or deeper without an adequate protective system, and some shallower trenches need one too.

lessons.title: Framing
lessons.short: Platform framing; studs, plates, headers, king and jack studs, cripples; joists and sheathing; engineered lumber; real lumber sizes.
lessons.intro: A wood-frame house has a skeleton of studs, joists and rafters, nailed together into floors, walls and a roof. This lesson names every piece, explains what each one does, and lets you frame a wall yourself.

blocks.html:
In platform framing, a house is built one floor at a time. The first floor’s joists sit on the foundation and are covered with subfloor panels, making a flat platform. Carpenters frame each wall flat on that platform, then stand it up and nail it in place. The next floor’s joists rest on top of those walls, making the next platform, and so on up to the roof.

Older houses were sometimes balloon framed, with walls whose studs run the entire height from the sill plate to the roof. Tall walls like that are heavy: OSHA reported 22 collapses of hand-raised balloon-framed walls from 1999 to 2004, which killed five workers and injured 28. In one, 15 workers were raising a wall that weighed about 2,300 pounds. OSHA’s advice is to plan the lift, work out the wall’s weight, and have a competent person supervise it.

blocks.html:
Wood swells as it absorbs water and shrinks as it dries, but only below its fiber saturation point, around 25 to 30 percent moisture content for most species. It shrinks very unevenly: dried all the way down, wood shrinks about 8 percent along the growth rings, about 4 percent across them, and only about 0.1 percent along its length.

Inside a house, wood slowly settles to a moisture content that matches the air around it: about 6 percent at 30 percent relative humidity and about 9 to 10 percent at 50 percent. So framing installed wetter than that shrinks a little as it dries, mostly in width and thickness and hardly at all in length. Wood kept below about 20 percent moisture is also less likely to be attacked by decay fungi and insects.

A wall is a bottom plate, a row of vertical studs, and a top plate. Traditionally, walls get a double top plate, and wood-framed houses have been built with 2×4 studs spaced 16 inches on center. Codes allow wider spacing in some cases, and the Department of Energy’s “advanced framing” approach uses 2×6 studs 24 inches on center: less wood, fewer thermal bridges, and more room for insulation.

“On center” means measured from the center of one stud to the center of the next. Carpenters mark the stud locations on the top and bottom plates together, so the studs line up. The same spacing is how a stud finder’s first hit helps you find the next one (Being an Adult 101).

Openings need extra parts. A header spans the top of a window or door opening and carries the load from above sideways to the studs on each side. A short jack stud under each end of the header holds it up, and a full-height king stud stands beside each jack. A window gets a rough sill at the bottom, and short cripple studs above the header and below the sill keep the on-center layout going so sheathing and drywall still land on wood. The header’s size comes from the code’s tables or an engineer; in a wall that carries no load, an open header can be used.

Framing parts and what they do
rows: Sill plate
Wood plate on top of the foundation, held down with anchor bolts or straps.
Rot or insect damage; air leaks at the joint.
Rim joist
Wraps the ends of the floor joists around the edge of the floor.
Drafts and cold floors where it isn’t sealed and insulated.
Floor joists
Span between supports and carry the floor.
Bounce, sag, cracks, notches cut by past repairs.
Subfloor
Sheathing panels that make the platform.
Squeaks, soft spots from water damage.
Bottom and top plates
Hold the studs in line and spread loads.
Rot at the bottom plate from leaks.
Studs
Carry loads down; give sheathing and drywall something to fasten to.
Cracks, holes cut too big for pipes or wires.
Header
Beam over an opening; carries the load to the jack studs.
Sagging over doors and windows; cracks at the corners.
King and jack studs
Frame the sides of an opening; jacks hold up the header.
Doors and windows that stick or go out of square.
Cripple studs
Short studs above headers and below sills that keep the layout.
Rarely a problem on their own.
Wall sheathing
Panels nailed to the studs that stiffen the wall against racking.
Rot from leaks behind siding.

blocks.html:
A floor starts with the sill plate anchored to the foundation, then a rim joist around the edge and floor joists spanning across, covered with subfloor panels. Air can leak in through the joints of the sill and rim joist, so those get sealed and insulated, with rigid foam cut to fit or with spray foam.

Walls get wall sheathing, often oriented strandboard (OSB): a structural panel made from thin wood strands bonded with water-resistant adhesive. Nailed to the studs, sheathing turns a wall into a stiff panel that resists racking, the triangle idea from Lesson 2.

Engineered wood products glue smaller pieces into bigger, more uniform ones:

  • Laminated veneer lumber (LVL) is made by laminating thin wood veneers with all the plies running the length of the piece. LVL is also used for the flanges of prefabricated I-joists.
  • I-joists look like a capital I: wide top and bottom flanges joined by a thin web. The flanges, far from the middle, do most of the work in bending, the same depth-matters idea as a deep joist.
  • Glued-laminated timber (glulam) is an engineered, stress-rated product of two or more layers of lumber glued together.

Engineered lumber comes with the manufacturer’s span and installation tables, and holes and notches may only go where those instructions allow.

It can be hard to tell. A wall may hold up joists, a beam, or a post from the floor above. Removing or cutting a load-bearing wall, beam, joist or header changes the load path. It needs a permit, and usually an engineer to design the new beam and posts and the footings under them.

Framing crews use nail guns, and OSHA reports about 37,000 emergency-room visits a year from them, most of them workers. The risk of injury is about twice as high with a multi-shot contact trigger as with a single-shot sequential trigger.

quiz.q: What is the actual size of a dry 2×4?
quiz.why: The name is the size before drying and planing. Dry 2×4s are 1½ inches by 3½ inches.

quiz.q: Which stud holds up the end of a header?
quiz.why: Jack studs stand under the ends of the header; king studs run full height beside them.

quiz.q: What do cripple studs do?
opts: Keep the stud layout going above headers and below sills
quiz.why: They keep wood on the on-center layout so sheathing and drywall can be fastened.

quiz.q: In which direction does wood shrink the least as it dries?
opts: It shrinks the same in every direction
quiz.why: About 0.1 percent along the length, compared with about 4 to 8 percent across the grain.

quiz.q: In platform framing, what do the walls of the second story stand on?
opts: The floor platform built on the first-story walls
quiz.why: Each floor is a platform, and the next story’s walls are built on it.

lessons.title: Roofs
lessons.short: Rafters and trusses, pitch, the layers from deck to shingles, flashing, attic ventilation, ice dams and gutters.
lessons.intro: A roof carries snow and wind, caps the attic, and sheds every drop of rain that lands on it. It’s built in layers, each lapped over the one below, so water always runs down and out.

blocks.html:
A roof’s frame is made of rafters or trusses. Rafters are sloped boards that run from the top of the wall up to a ridge at the peak. A truss is a frame made entirely of triangles: top chords along the roof slope, a bottom chord that also serves as the ceiling joist, and webs between them. As Lesson 2 showed, triangles can’t rack, so a truss turns the roof’s loads into tension and compression in its members.

Truss shapes vary. A raised-heel truss stands taller where it sits on the wall, leaving room for full-depth attic insulation all the way out to the eaves, which helps prevent ice dams. Trusses can also span long distances, which can remove the need for some interior load-bearing walls.

Every member of a truss is part of its design, so cutting or notching even a small web can weaken the whole truss. Repairs or changes need the truss designer or an engineer.

Roof slope, or pitch, is written as inches of rise for every 12 inches of run: a “6 in 12” roof climbs 6 inches for every foot it goes across. The angle and the length of a rafter come straight from right-triangle geometry.

OSHA sorts roofs by slope for its fall-protection rules: a low-slope roof is 4 in 12 or less, and anything steeper is a steep roof. Steep-slope roofs are typical on single-family homes; low-slope roofs are most common on commercial, industrial and apartment buildings.
angle = tan⁻¹(rise ÷ 12)    rafter length = run × √(12² + rise²) ÷ 12

blocks.cap: Choose a pitch and the building’s width. The rafter length is measured along the slope from the ridge to the tail of the overhang; real layout also allows for the ridge board and the seat cut where the rafter sits on the wall.

blocks.h: The layers, from the deck up
blocks.html:
• Roof deck: sheathing panels nailed to the rafters or trusses.
  • Ice and water membrane: in climate zone 5 and colder, a self-sealing membrane goes along the eaves, from the roof edge to at least 2 feet inside the plane of the interior wall, lapped over the metal drip edge. If an ice dam backs water up under the shingles, the membrane keeps it out of the attic.
  • Peel-and-stick in valleys and at walls: the valleys and the places where a roof meets a wall are among the most vulnerable spots, so they get a membrane too.
  • Underlayment: roofing felt or another underlayment over the rest of the deck, a second line of defense under the shingles.
  • Drip edge: metal at the eaves and rakes that guides water off the edge.
  • Roofing: asphalt shingles are common on homes; metal, tile and slate are others. Each course of shingles laps over the one below.

blocks.h: Flashing: where the roof meets something else
blocks.html:
Flashing is sheet metal or membrane that bridges a joint water could otherwise get into. Step flashing goes wherever a roof meets a wall, such as a dormer: corrosion-resistant pieces at least 4 inches up the wall and 4 inches onto the deck, woven in shingle fashion so each upper layer laps over the one below. At the bottom of a roof-wall joint, a kick-out flashing (diverter) turns the water out into the gutter instead of letting it run down inside the wall. Chimneys, vent pipes and every other penetration get flashing too.

The edges of a roof take the hardest beating from wind: they see the highest pushes and pulls of air pressure, so roof edges in high-wind areas get extra attention.

blocks.cap: Roof parts and what they do
rows: Rafters or trusses
Carry the roof’s weight, snow and wind down to the walls.
Sagging ridge or roof plane; cut or cracked members.
Roof deck
Sheathing that the roofing is nailed to.
Soft spots, stains, rot from long-term leaks.
Ice and water membrane
Seals the eaves, valleys and roof-wall joints against backed-up water.
Leaks at the eaves during ice-dam season.
Underlayment
A water-resistant layer under the roofing.
Shows through where shingles are missing.
Shingles or metal
Shed water; each course laps over the one below.
Curling, missing or broken shingles; granules in gutters.
Step and kick-out flashing
Seal roof-to-wall joints and steer water into the gutter.
Stains on walls below a roof-wall joint; rot.
Drip edge
Guides water off the roof edge.
Rot at the fascia and roof edge.
Soffit and ridge vents
Let outside air in at the eaves and out at the peak.
Frost or mold in the attic; ice dams.
Baffles
Keep an air channel open above the insulation at the eaves.
Insulation blocking the soffit vents.
Gutters and downspouts
Collect roof water and carry it away from the foundation.
Overflowing, sagging, water at the foundation.

blocks.html:
A vented attic breathes. Outside air comes in through vents in the soffits under the eaves and leaves through a vent along the ridge. In each rafter bay with a soffit vent, a rigid chute called a baffle keeps an air gap between the insulation and the roof deck and steers air up toward the ridge.

Without good ventilation, moisture can build up in an attic, causing mold, ruining insulation and damaging wood. Bathroom fans, kitchen range hoods and clothes dryers must vent all the way outdoors, never into the attic: that is a bad practice that can lead to mold, and it may violate local codes.

An ice dam is a ridge of ice at the edge of a roof that keeps melting snow from draining off. It takes three things together: snow on the roof, an upper roof that’s above 32 °F, and lower edges that stay below freezing. Heat leaking from the house warms the upper roof, snow melts there, and the water refreezes when it reaches the cold eaves. Water that backs up behind the dam can work under the shingles and leak into walls, ceilings and insulation, and the dampness can lead to mold.

blocks.html:
University of Minnesota Extension says the long-term fix starts inside: make the ceiling airtight so warm, moist air can’t leak into the attic, then consider adding insulation. Natural ventilation helps keep the roof evenly cold, but once heat loss is cut, only a little is needed, and Extension does not recommend mechanical attic ventilation as a solution to ice dams. A weatherization contractor can find the leaks with a blower door test and an infrared camera.

In the short term, removing snow takes away one ingredient, but a roof rake or push broom can damage roofing, and anyone working on a roof in winter risks injury. Extension suggests hiring professionals for that work.

OSHA calls falls the leading cause of death in construction: in 2024, 389 of 1,034 construction deaths were falls to a lower level. From 2003 to 2013, falls from roofs alone accounted for about a third of construction fall deaths. Workers on roofs and other surfaces 6 feet or more above a lower level must be protected by guardrails, safety nets or personal fall arrest systems. Leave roof work to roofers with the training and equipment, and look at your roof from the ground.

blocks.h: Signs of water getting into the roof edge
blocks.html: The Department of Energy’s Guide to Durable Attics lists warning signs: warped or rotted soffits or fascia boards, bubbled paint on the fascia or soffits, worn or warped shingles at the roof edge, wet attic insulation near the eaves, mold or mildew on attic surfaces, and warped or rotting attic wood.

lessons.title: The Building Envelope
lessons.short: Controlling water, air, vapor and heat: drainage planes and flashing, air sealing, vapor retarders, insulation and R-values, windows.
lessons.intro: The envelope is everything that separates inside from outside: the foundation, walls, windows, doors and roof. A good one controls four things: liquid water, air, water vapor and heat. This lesson takes them one at a time.

blocks.html: Moisture moves into a wall four ways: as bulk water (rain, snowmelt, groundwater), by capillary wicking through porous materials, carried along by air that leaks through, and by vapor slowly diffusing through materials. Heat moves too, by conduction, convection and radiation. Each needs its own control layer, and the layers have to work together. Try each one here.

blocks.cap: Pick a tab. Water: remove the barrier to see what happens. Air: leave a gap at the outlet. Vapor and heat: change the outdoor temperature and add foam sheathing. The heat numbers use OpenStax’s R-11 for 3½-inch batts and about R-1.2 per inch for wood; drywall, paint and air films are left out.

blocks.html:
Siding sheds most rain, but some always gets behind it. So behind the siding there’s a weather-resistive barrier (WRB): house wrap, building paper, taped foam sheathing or a coating that’s sprayed or rolled on. Together with the flashing and the roofing, it forms the drainage plane. University of Minnesota Extension puts the rule simply: “Every element of the drainage plane must be installed so it will direct water out and over the layer below it.” Layers are lapped like shingles, and tape is no substitute for lapping them the right way.

Every hole in a wall is a chance for a leak, and a house typically has 20 or more of them on its outside walls: pipes, vents, wires, lights and more. Each one has to be flashed into the drainage plane. Windows and doors are the biggest interruptions, and leaks around them often aren’t found until damage has already happened inside the wall.

blocks.html: Window flashing goes on in shingle order: sill flashing first, then the sides lapped over it, then the head flashing, and finally the house wrap above folds down over the head flashing. The sides and top of the window’s flange get sealed, but the outside of the bottom flange should not be caulked or taped: water that gets into the window opening has to be able to drain back out.

Air leaks make a house drafty, put extra strain on heating and cooling equipment, and let in moisture that can damage wood and encourage mold. The Department of Energy compares the two jobs this way: insulation slows heat flow, but “air sealing acts like a windbreaker.” Air leaks are among the greatest sources of energy loss in a home, and DOE says sealing and weatherizing can save 10 to 20 percent on heating and cooling bills.

The usual leaks are around windows and doors, between the attic and the rooms below, where siding meets the foundation, and wherever pipes, vents, wires, ducts and fans pass through outside walls. Walls and rim joists make up more than 40 percent of a home’s envelope area, so they matter too. Caulk seals cracks and gaps; spray foam fills bigger ones; weatherstripping seals doors and the moving parts of windows. Gaps near chimneys, flues and furnace vents need special high-temperature materials, a job DOE suggests leaving to a pro.

blocks.h: Vapor: put the retarder on the warm side
blocks.html:
A vapor retarder slows how fast water vapor moves through a material. They come in three classes by permeance: Class I at 0.1 perm or less, Class II between 0.1 and 1.0 perm, and Class III at 1.0 perm or more. Vapor retarders belong closest to the warm side of a wall: the inside in cold climates, the outside in hot, humid ones. No vapor barrier is required in mild or hot climates; the building code requires them in colder climates (zones 5 through 8), where a Class II or Class III retarder such as kraft-faced insulation or latex paint is often enough.

A vapor retarder doesn’t stop air. Moisture carried by leaking air needs an air barrier, which is why air sealing and vapor control go together. Lesson 10 shows how vapor becomes liquid water at a cold surface.

Heat moves three ways: by conduction through solid materials, by convection as air or another fluid moves, and by radiation. Most insulation slows heat flow by conduction and convection: its fibers or foam cells hold air still, and still air conducts heat poorly (OpenStax lists air at 0.023 watts per meter-kelvin). The rate of heat flow through a layer depends on its area, the temperature difference across it, its thickness, and its thermal conductivity. Builders combine thickness and conductivity into one number, the R-value: the larger the R, the better it insulates. R-values of layers in a row add up.
heat flow per square foot = (T<sub>inside</sub> − T<sub>outside</sub>) ÷ R  <small>(Q/t = kA(T₂ − T₁)/d, with R = d/k)</small>

• Batts and rolls (blankets) of mineral fibers such as fiberglass, sized to fit between standard stud and joist spacing. OpenStax gives about R-11 for 3½-inch fiberglass batts, used in walls, and R-19 for 6½-inch batts, used in ceilings.
  • Loose-fill fiberglass, rock wool or cellulose, blown in with special equipment; good for attics and odd-shaped spaces with wires and pipes in the way.
  • Foam-in-place (spray foam), which insulates and also reduces air leakage through holes and cracks.
  • Rigid foam board, used as exterior wall sheathing and on basement walls.

Installed insulation can perform below its rated R-value if it has gaps, voids or compressed spots, or if air moves through it. And wood conducts heat two to four times better than glass wool (0.08 to 0.16 versus 0.042 watts per meter-kelvin), so every stud is a small thermal bridge through the insulation.

blocks.html:
Windows are rated by the National Fenestration Rating Council (NFRC), and its label lets you compare products. Two numbers matter most:

  • U-factor is the rate at which a window, door or skylight lets non-solar heat flow through. The lower the U-factor, the more energy-efficient it is.
  • Solar heat gain coefficient (SHGC) is the fraction of the sun’s radiation that gets through. The lower the SHGC, the less solar heat comes in. ENERGY STAR suggests a low SHGC, or shading, for windows that face east and west.

ENERGY STAR sets limits for each climate region. It says certified windows lower household energy bills by an average of up to 13 percent nationwide when they replace single-pane windows.

blocks.h: Before you tighten up a house
blocks.html:
DOE says the first step in air sealing is working out how much fresh air the home needs. Without proper ventilation, moisture and harmful combustion gases can build up, and fuel-burning appliances that don’t get enough air may release carbon monoxide into the home. A professional energy auditor or certified HVAC contractor can test the house.

In an attic, watch for vermiculite: loose, pebbly insulation. EPA lists attic and wall insulation containing vermiculite among the products that may contain asbestos. Leave it alone, and if you plan work that could disturb it, have it checked by a trained, accredited asbestos professional first.

lessons.title: Interior Finishes and Stairs
lessons.short: Drywall and why it slows fire, taping and mud, trim and doors, flooring, paint, and how stairs are laid out.
lessons.intro: Finishes are the parts you see and touch: drywall, trim, doors, floors, paint and stairs. They go in last, after the house is weather-tight and the work inside the walls has been inspected.

blocks.html:
Drywall (gypsum board) is a sheet of gypsum pressed between two layers of heavy paper. Installers measure, mark and cut the panels to fit the plans, fasten them to the studs and ceiling framing, and then tapers cover the joints. The work often means lifting heavy panels overhead to fasten them to the ceiling.

Drywall also slows fire. Gypsum is calcium sulfate with water molecules locked into its crystals, about 20 percent of its weight, and it takes a lot of heat to drive that water out. The Being an Adult 101 guide to patching drywall explains the chemistry.

blocks.html:
The long edges of a drywall sheet are slightly tapered, so where two sheets meet there’s a shallow channel. Tapers bed paper or fiberglass mesh tape in joint compound (“mud”) across the joint, then add more coats, each a little wider and thinner, and sand between coats until the joint disappears. Screw heads get the same treatment. Thin coats dry faster than thick ones, and compound shrinks a little as it dries, which is why a deep fill may need a second coat.

Sanding makes fine dust, so keep it contained and protect your eyes and lungs. In older homes there’s more to think about, as the Stop box below explains.

Trim covers the joints where drywall meets windows, doors and floors: casing around openings, baseboard along the floor, and sometimes crown molding at the ceiling. Installing windows, doors and molding is part of a carpenter’s job. Doors and windows only work smoothly when their frames are plumb (perfectly vertical) and square, which is why the framing and the measuring in Lesson 8 matter so much.

Finish flooring goes over the subfloor: wood, tile, vinyl or carpet, each with its own underlayment and installation instructions from the manufacturer. Flooring installers and tile and stone setters are their own trade.

Old flooring deserves care. EPA lists vinyl floor tiles, the backing on vinyl sheet flooring, and their adhesives among the products that may contain asbestos, and says you generally can’t tell whether a material contains asbestos just by looking at it.

New drywall and patches get primer first, then paint, so the color and sheen come out even. Paint is part of the envelope too: in cold climates, latex paint on the inside of an exterior wall can serve as a Class III vapor retarder (Lesson 6).

Old paint is a hazard to plan for. If a home was built before 1978, it may have lead-based paint, and the older the home, the more likely it is.

• Lead: EPA requires anyone paid to do work that disturbs paint in homes and child-care facilities built before 1978 to be certified and to follow lead-safe work practices. Minor jobs that disturb 6 square feet or less of paint per room inside, or 20 square feet or less outside, are exempt, but window replacement and demolition of painted surfaces are always covered. The rule generally doesn’t apply to homeowners working in their own homes, but EPA urges them to work lead-safe: test first or assume lead is present, contain the work area, use power tools with HEPA vacuum attachments, and clean up with a HEPA vacuum and wet wiping.
  • Asbestos: material in good condition that won’t be disturbed should be left alone. Before a remodel that could disturb it, have it inspected. Don’t dust, sweep or vacuum debris that may contain asbestos.

A stair is a set of risers (the vertical part of each step) and treads (the part you step on), carried by sloped boards called stringers. The front edge of a tread is the nosing. Codes also cover handrails, guards along open sides, and headroom above.

Laying out a stair starts with the total rise: the height from one finished floor to the next. Divide it by the tallest riser the local code allows and round up to get the number of risers; then divide the total rise by that number so every riser comes out exactly the same. There’s always one fewer tread than risers, because the upper floor is the last step. The local code sets the limits for riser height, tread depth, headroom, handrails and guards, and those rules vary from place to place.

lessons.title: Reading Plans and Measuring
lessons.short: Plans, elevations and sections, scale and symbols, squaring a corner with 3-4-5, level and plumb, and estimating materials.
lessons.intro: Builders turn drawings into buildings with a tape measure, a level and a little math. This lesson shows how to read a set of plans and the measuring tricks every carpenter uses, with calculators you can try.

blocks.html:
Following blueprints and building plans is the first duty the Bureau of Labor Statistics lists for carpenters. A set of plans shows the same house several ways:

  • Plan views look straight down on each floor, as if the house were sliced through partway up the walls. They show walls, doors, windows, stairs and room sizes, with dimensions.
  • Elevations show each outside face of the house: heights, roof slope, windows and siding.
  • Sections show the house sliced open, so you can see how the foundation, floors, walls and roof go together.
  • Details zoom in on one spot, such as a stair or a window, at a larger scale.

Plans also go to the building department, where a plans examiner checks them against the adopted codes before a permit is issued.

blocks.html: Drawings are made to scale. At a scale of ¼ inch = 1 foot, every quarter inch on the paper stands for a foot of the house, so a 24-foot wall is drawn 6 inches long. When a dimension is written on the plans, use the number rather than measuring the paper, since copies aren’t always printed at true size.
real length = drawn length × scale factor  <small>at ¼″ = 1′, the factor is 48 (1 foot ÷ ¼ inch = 12 ÷ 0.25)</small>

Builders in the United States measure in feet and inches, and they split inches into halves, quarters, eighths and sixteenths. On plans, 12′-6″ means 12 feet 6 inches. Adding fractions comes up all the time: a stud 1½ inches thick plus a 3⅝-inch gap is 5⅛ inches. Converting everything to sixteenths (1½ = 24/16, 3⅝ = 58/16, total 82/16 = 5 2/16 = 5⅛) is one reliable way to do it in your head.

Foundation forms, walls and decks need square (90-degree) corners. The trick is the Pythagorean theorem: in a right triangle, the square of the long side equals the sum of the squares of the other two. Since 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5², a triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 always has a right angle.

So measure 3 feet along one line from the corner and mark it, 4 feet along the other and mark it, and measure between the marks. If the diagonal is exactly 5 feet, the corner is square. If it’s long, the corner is more than 90 degrees; if it’s short, less. Any multiple works too, such as 6-8-10 or 9-12-15, and a bigger triangle makes a small error easier to see on the tape.

blocks.cap: Press Measure, then knock the corner out of square and measure again. The law of cosines gives the diagonal when the angle isn’t 90°: c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos θ.

blocks.html: For a rectangle, such as a slab form or a deck, measure both diagonals from corner to corner. If the opposite sides are equal and the two diagonals are equal, the rectangle is square. If one diagonal is longer, nudge the frame toward the shorter one.

Level means perfectly horizontal and plumb means perfectly vertical. A spirit level has a curved vial of liquid with an air bubble; the bubble rises to the highest point, so it sits between the lines only when the level is flat (Being an Adult 101 explains why). A plumb bob is just a weight on a string: gravity pulls it straight down, toward the center of the Earth, so the string hangs exactly vertical. Lasers do the same jobs over longer distances.

Estimating is mostly multiplication and division. Concrete is ordered by volume, in cubic yards: one cubic yard is 3 feet × 3 feet × 3 feet, or 27 cubic feet. Drywall is ordered by the sheet: the area to cover divided by the area of one sheet. Studs follow from the wall length and the spacing. Builders add a margin for cuts and mistakes, and suppliers sell in their own sizes, so check before you order.
cubic yards = length (ft) × width (ft) × thickness (ft) ÷ 27  <small>a 4-inch slab is 4/12 = 0.333 ft thick</small>

blocks.cap: Change the sizes and the margin. The pictures show the quantity: one block per cubic yard, one panel per sheet, one stick per stud.

blocks.html: The old saying is still the best advice. Write measurements down, mark which side of the line to cut on, and check a cut piece against the space before you nail it in.

quiz.q: At a scale of ¼ inch = 1 foot, how long is a wall drawn 6 inches long?
quiz.why: Six inches is 24 quarter-inches, and each quarter-inch is a foot.

quiz.q: You measure 6 feet and 8 feet along two lines from a corner. If the corner is square, the diagonal between the marks is…
The diagonal of your 3-4-5 check comes out longer than 5 feet. The corner is…
quiz.why: A wider angle opens the triangle, so the diagonal gets longer.

quiz.q: About how many cubic yards of concrete is a 20 × 12 foot slab, 4 inches thick, before any extra?
quiz.why: 20 × 12 × 0.333 = 80 cubic feet, and 80 ÷ 27 ≈ 2.96 cubic yards.

quiz.q: Which drawing shows how the foundation, floors, walls and roof go together?
quiz.why: A section slices the house open to show the layers.

lessons.intro: OSHA, the federal workplace safety agency, calls construction a high-hazard industry. Most of the danger comes from a handful of well-understood hazards. Here’s what OSHA’s rules and guidance say about each one.

blocks.html: OSHA puts it plainly: “The top four causes of construction fatalities are: Falls, Struck-By, Caught-In/Between and Electrocutions.” OSHA’s training calls them the Construction Focus Four, and every 10- and 30-hour construction Outreach course has to cover them. Falls lead the list. In 2024, 389 of the 1,034 construction workers who died on the job were killed in falls to a lower level.

blocks.html:
In residential construction, OSHA’s standard says each worker 6 feet or more above a lower level must be protected by a guardrail system, a safety net system or a personal fall arrest system. OSHA also allows an effective fall restraint system in place of fall arrest. Some details from OSHA’s guidance for roofing work:

  • A personal fall arrest system is an anchor, a full-body harness, and a lifeline or lanyard. The anchor should go into a structural member, not just the sheathing. Body belts aren’t allowed for fall arrest.
  • The top rails of a guardrail system must be 39 to 45 inches above the walking surface.
  • Covers over holes and skylights must hold at least twice the load expected on them, be secured, and be marked “HOLE” or “COVER.”

OSHA’s campaign boils fall prevention down to three words: Plan ahead, Provide the right equipment, and Train everyone to use it.

OSHA’s ladder rules for construction include these:

  • Set an extension ladder so its base is about one-quarter of its working length out from the wall (4 up for every 1 out).
  • When a ladder is used to get onto a roof or other landing, its side rails must extend at least 3 feet above the landing.
  • Face the ladder when climbing up or down, keep three points of contact (two hands and a foot, or two feet and a hand), and don’t carry tools in your hands while climbing.
  • Never use the top or top step of a stepladder as a step.
  • Use ladders only for what they were designed for, and don’t lay an extension ladder flat as a platform.
  • Keep ladders and other tools at least 10 feet from power lines, and use ladders with nonconductive side rails where they could touch energized electrical equipment.
  • Inspect ladders before use. Mark a damaged ladder “Do Not Use” and take it out of service until it’s repaired.

blocks.html:
To prevent struck-by injuries, OSHA says never to position yourself between moving and fixed objects, and to wear high-visibility clothing near equipment and vehicles.

Trenches are the classic caught-in hazard. OSHA’s rules:

  • Trenches 5 feet deep or more need a protective system (sloping, shoring, benching or a trench shield), unless they’re dug entirely in stable rock. Some shallower trenches need one too.
  • Trenches 20 feet deep or more need a protective system designed by a registered professional engineer, or based on tabulated data a professional engineer prepared or approved.
  • Keep excavated soil and other materials at least 2 feet back from the edge.
  • A competent person must inspect trenches daily and as conditions change, before anyone goes in. Trenches more than 4 feet deep get tested for low oxygen and toxic gases.

OSHA’s precautions: locate and identify utilities before starting work; look for overhead power lines when operating any equipment and keep a safe distance from them; use portable electric tools only if they are grounded or double-insulated; use ground-fault circuit interrupters (GFCIs); and be alert to electrical hazards when working on ladders, scaffolds or other platforms. The Electrical course explains how GFCIs work.

OSHA’s five basic rules for hand and power tools: keep tools in good condition with regular maintenance; use the right tool for the job; examine each tool for damage before use, and don’t use damaged tools; operate tools according to the manufacturer’s instructions; and use the right personal protective equipment. Also:

  • Never carry a tool by its cord or hose.
  • Disconnect tools when they’re not in use, before servicing or cleaning them, and when changing blades, bits or other accessories.
  • Never remove safety guards while the tool is in use. A portable circular saw needs an upper guard over the whole blade and a lower guard that retracts as it cuts and springs back when the saw is lifted out.
  • Clamp or vise the work so both hands are free for the tool, and keep good footing and balance.

Nail guns cause an estimated 37,000 emergency-room visits a year, and they put more construction workers in the hospital than any other tool. OSHA says the risk of injury is twice as high with a multi-shot contact trigger as with a single-shot sequential trigger.

Personal protective equipment, or PPE, is gear worn to reduce exposure to hazards: gloves, safety glasses and shoes, earplugs or muffs, hard hats, respirators, coveralls and vests. OSHA treats it as the protection to use when engineering, work-practice and administrative controls aren’t feasible or aren’t enough on their own. Employers must provide PPE and train workers in when it’s needed and how to wear it. The Bureau of Labor Statistics says carpenters typically wear boots, hard hats, eye protection and reflective vests.

Silica. Quartz is a basic component of sand and granite, and cutting, drilling or grinding concrete, brick, block or stone throws up fine crystalline silica dust. OSHA says breathing it causes silicosis, an incurable lung disease that leads to disability and death, as well as lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and kidney disease. Controls include saws that feed water continuously to the blade, ventilation, a HEPA-filtered wet vacuum for the slurry, and respirators.

Lead. Homes built before 1978 may have lead-based paint. Anyone paid to disturb paint in those homes must be EPA-certified and work lead-safe (Lesson 7).

Asbestos. EPA says you generally can’t tell whether a material contains asbestos just by looking at it. Leave material in good condition alone, have it inspected before a remodel that could disturb it, and never dust, sweep or vacuum debris that may contain it.

Fall arrest equipment, perimeter protection, secured and labeled covers over floor openings, ladders and scaffolds used safely.

blocks.h: Know when the job needs more than you have
blocks.html: Work at height, trenches, structural demolition and anything involving lead paint or possible asbestos need training, equipment and often certification. If the job needs fall protection you don’t have or know how to use, a trench box, or a respirator fitted to you, it belongs with a trained crew.

quiz.q: Which four hazards does OSHA call the top causes of construction deaths?
opts: Falls, struck-by, caught-in or between, and electrocution
Ladders, saws, drills and nail guns
quiz.why: OSHA’s Focus Four. Falls are the leading cause.

quiz.q: In residential construction, OSHA requires fall protection for workers how high above a lower level?
quiz.why: 6 feet or more: guardrails, safety nets or personal fall arrest systems.

quiz.q: When you climb an extension ladder onto a roof, its side rails must extend how far above the roof edge?
quiz.why: At least 3 feet above the upper landing.

quiz.q: At what depth does OSHA require a protective system for a trench, unless it’s in stable rock?
quiz.why: 5 feet or more, and some shallower trenches need one too. At 20 feet, an engineer designs it.

quiz.q: Which nail gun trigger carries about half the injury risk of a multi-shot contact trigger?
opts: Any trigger with the safety removed
quiz.why: OSHA says the risk is twice as high with a multi-shot contact trigger.

lessons.title: Moisture, Mold and Building Science
lessons.short: Where the water comes from, how it moves, why cold surfaces sweat, how mold grows, and the details that keep a house dry.
lessons.intro: A lot of what goes wrong with houses comes back to water. This lesson explains where it comes from, the four ways it moves, why cold surfaces sweat, and how good details keep wood dry and mold away.

blocks.html:
University of Minnesota Extension sorts the moisture in a house into three sources: liquid water from rain or groundwater; moisture made inside the house by cooking, bathing, unvented clothes dryers and humidifiers; and humid outdoor air that gets in and condenses on cooler surfaces. Plumbing leaks add a fourth, and new construction adds a fifth: fresh concrete gives off about 0.2 gallons of water per square foot of wall and 0.1 gallons per square foot of floor as it dries.

The amounts can be big. A 1-inch rain drops about 1,250 gallons on the roof of a 2,000-square-foot house.

• Bulk water flows: rain, snowmelt, groundwater, leaks. Gravity drives it, so the fix is to direct it away and lap every layer so water runs out over the one below.
  • Capillary water wicks through tiny pores, up into concrete or along wood, even uphill. Gravel and plastic sheeting under a slab are capillary breaks. In soil, capillary water can climb a few inches in gravel and as much as 12 to 20 feet in clay.
  • Air-carried moisture rides along with air leaking through gaps. An air barrier stops it.
  • Vapor diffusion is water vapor moving slowly through materials. Vapor retarders slow it.

blocks.html:
Air can hold only so much water vapor, and warm air can hold much more than cold air. Relative humidity is how much vapor the air holds compared with the most it could hold at that temperature. Cool that air without adding or removing any water and its relative humidity rises, until at the dew point it reaches 100 percent. Any surface colder than the dew point collects condensation.

That’s why windows fog and drip on cold nights, why cold-water pipes sweat in summer, and why basement walls get damp when warm, humid summer air comes in and meets the cool concrete. University of Minnesota Extension notes that people often think that last one is a leak when it’s really condensation.

blocks.cap: Pick a scenario or set your own room temperature, humidity and surface temperature. The curve is how much water vapor air can hold at each temperature, from OpenStax’s table. The room air slides left at constant moisture until it hits the curve: that’s the dew point.

blocks.html:
EPA’s first rule: “The key to mold control is moisture control.” Mold can grow on almost anything that stays damp, and a musty smell is sometimes the only clue. EPA’s advice:

  • Dry water-damaged areas and items within 24 to 48 hours to prevent mold growth, and fix plumbing leaks and other water problems as soon as possible.
  • Keep indoor relative humidity below 60 percent, ideally between 30 and 50 percent.
  • Reduce condensation: insulate cold surfaces such as cold-water pipes, vent clothes dryers, stoves and other moisture-producing appliances outdoors, and run bathroom and kitchen fans.
  • Clean and repair gutters, and slope the ground away from the foundation.
  • If the moldy area is less than about 10 square feet, many homeowners can clean it up themselves following EPA’s guidance. Clean up the mold and fix the water problem; cleaning alone lets it come back.
  • Absorbent materials such as ceiling tiles and carpet may have to be thrown away if they get moldy. Don’t paint or caulk over mold.
  • Don’t run the heating and cooling system if you know or suspect it’s contaminated with mold.

Mold can cause allergic reactions in sensitive people, irritate the eyes, skin, nose, throat and lungs, and trigger asthma attacks in people with asthma who are allergic to it.

Wood is food for decay fungi when it stays wet. Wood kept below about 20 percent moisture content is less susceptible to fungi and insects, and dry indoor wood sits far below that (Lesson 4). Rot starts where wood stays wet: behind siding with no drainage plane, under a window with no sill flashing, below a roof-wall joint with no kick-out flashing, on a sill plate over a damp foundation, or on crawlspace joists above bare soil. Water intrusion around windows and doors often isn’t discovered until damage has already happened inside the wall.

The detail that prevents it

A lapped weather-resistive barrier and flashing: a drainage plane.
Leaks under windows
Sill flashing first, sides next, head last; don’t seal the bottom flange.

Step flashing and a kick-out flashing that steers water into the gutter.

Gutters, downspout extensions and soil sloped away from the house; drain tile.

A capillary break: gravel and sealed plastic sheeting.

Air sealing the ceiling, insulation, ventilation, fans vented outdoors.
Condensation inside walls
Air sealing, a vapor retarder on the warm side where the code calls for one, and a warmer sheathing.
Mold in bathrooms
An exhaust fan vented outdoors, used during and after showers.

blocks.html:
• Run bathroom and kitchen fans, and make sure the dryer vents outdoors.
  • Keep an eye on indoor humidity with an inexpensive hygrometer, and aim for 30 to 50 percent.
  • Fix drips fast, and dry anything wet within 24 to 48 hours.
  • Know where to shut off the water (Being an Adult 101).

blocks.h: Call a pro for big water and big mold
blocks.html: For heavy water damage or mold over about 10 square feet, EPA points to its professional remediation guidance. If you hire a contractor, EPA says to make sure they have experience cleaning up mold. If you have health concerns, talk to a health professional before you start any cleanup.

quiz.q: According to EPA, what is the key to mold control?
quiz.why: “The key to mold control is moisture control.” Fix the water problem, or the mold comes back.

quiz.q: EPA says to dry water-damaged areas within…
quiz.why: Within 24 to 48 hours, to prevent mold growth.

quiz.q: What indoor relative humidity does EPA suggest?
quiz.why: Below 60 percent, ideally between 30 and 50 percent.

quiz.q: The dew point is the temperature at which…
opts: air cooled at constant moisture reaches 100% relative humidity
quiz.why: Below the dew point, vapor condenses into liquid water on a surface.

quiz.q: A basement wall is damp in humid summer weather, even with no rain. The likely cause is…
opts: humid air condensing on the cool wall
quiz.why: University of Minnesota Extension says this is often condensation, not a leak.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting a House by Symptom
lessons.short: An interactive finder: pick a symptom, answer a question, and see the likely causes, safe checks, and when to call a pro or engineer.
lessons.intro: Houses tell you when something is wrong: a crack, a stain, a door that sticks, a musty smell. Use the finder to narrow down the cause, learn what you can safely check, and know when it’s time for a licensed pro or an engineer.

blocks.html:
• Follow the water. Many house problems involve water somewhere. Work from the outside in: roof, gutters, grading, siding, windows, then the inside.
  • Notice the timing. Only after rain? Only in winter? Only in humid weather? The timing often points straight at the cause.
  • Watch for change. Mark both ends of a crack with a pencil line and the date, and take a photo. A crack that stays the same is very different from one that grows.
  • Look, don’t open. Check what you can see safely from the ground, from inside, or from the attic or basement. Leave roofs, structure, and anything that might contain lead paint or asbestos alone until you know more.

blocks.h: Cracks: which are common and which aren’t
blocks.html:
Concrete shrinks a little as it dries, and that shrinking pulls on it from inside. University of Minnesota Extension says concrete and concrete-block foundations usually develop some cracks, and that drainage usually removes the water from them, though repair may be needed. A thin crack that stays the same size is common.

Drywall moves too. Wood framing shrinks as it dries and swells and shrinks a little with the seasons, so small cracks at corners and joints and the occasional nail pop are common in houses, and they’re easy to patch.

Other signs call for a professional: a crack that keeps getting wider or longer, one side of a crack that has moved out of line with the other, a foundation wall that bows or leans, floors that sag more over time, or doors and windows that suddenly start to bind. Have a structural engineer or an experienced foundation contractor look. Repairs to structure need a permit.

If water is coming from a broken pipe, shut off the main water valve (Being an Adult 101 shows how) and call a plumber. Then dry everything you can within 24 to 48 hours, as EPA advises, to head off mold.

lessons.title: Doing Your Own Work
lessons.short: A starter tool kit, working safely, permits, and the skill ladder from first jobs to the work that belongs to licensed contractors and engineers.
lessons.intro: Plenty of house work is within reach of a careful beginner, and some of it isn’t. This lesson covers a starter tool kit, how to work safely, when a permit comes in, and a skill ladder from first jobs to the jobs that belong to licensed contractors and engineers.

blocks.html:
• Measuring and marking: a 25-foot tape measure, a pencil, a 2-foot or 4-foot level, a speed square or combination square, and a stud finder.
  • Fastening: a hammer, screwdrivers, and a cordless drill-driver with bits.
  • Cutting: a utility knife and a handsaw; a circular saw when you’re ready for it.
  • Finishing: putty knives, a sanding sponge, caulk and a caulk gun.
  • Protection: safety glasses, hearing protection, work gloves, and dust masks or a fitted respirator for dusty jobs.

The first jobs in hanging a picture and patching drywall use most of these.

blocks.h: Work the way the pros are taught
blocks.html:
OSHA’s basic tool rules apply at home too: keep tools in good condition; use the right tool for the job; examine each tool before use and don’t use a damaged one; follow the manufacturer’s instructions; and wear the right protective gear. Unplug a tool before changing a blade or bit, never carry it by the cord, leave the guards on, and clamp the work so both hands are free.

On ladders, set the base about a quarter of the working length out, extend the rails 3 feet above any landing you step onto, face the ladder, and keep three points of contact. In a house built before 1978, assume painted surfaces may contain lead and work lead-safe. If you’re about to cut into old flooring, ceiling texture or insulation, find out first whether it might contain asbestos.

Which jobs need a permit depends on where you live, so the first step is a call to your city or county building department. Changes to structure (walls, beams, foundations, roof framing), additions, and new or enlarged openings commonly need one, and so does most electrical, plumbing and gas work. A permit isn’t just paperwork: the plan review and the inspections are a second set of trained eyes on work that will be hidden inside the walls.

blocks.h: Jobs for licensed contractors and engineers
blocks.html:
Some work belongs with professionals because the consequences of a mistake are serious, because it takes equipment and training a homeowner doesn’t have, or because the law requires a license or certification:

  • Structure: removing or changing a load-bearing wall, beam, header, post or truss; foundation repairs. These need a permit and usually an engineer’s design.
  • Roofs: roof work means working at height, where OSHA requires fall protection for workers at 6 feet and up.
  • Excavation: trenches 5 feet or deeper need a protective system.
  • Lead and asbestos: paid work that disturbs paint in pre-1978 homes needs EPA certification; suspected asbestos needs a trained, accredited professional.
  • Big mold and water jobs: mold over about 10 square feet or after heavy water damage.
  • The other trades’ licensed work: gas piping, the electrical panel and service, and refrigerant handling. See the Plumbing, Electrical and HVAC courses.

Hiring? Many states and cities license building contractors, so check a contractor’s license with your state or local licensing office.
Before you open a wall, find out what’s inside it. Pipes, wires and ducts can be anywhere, and the wall itself may be holding up the house. When you’re not sure, stop and ask a pro.

lessons.title: Careers in Construction
lessons.short: What carpenters do, what they earn, the job outlook, apprenticeships, OSHA 10- and 30-hour training, and related careers.
lessons.intro: Building houses is skilled work, and many people learn it on the job while getting paid. This lesson uses the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ figures for carpenters, then looks at training, safety courses and related careers.

blocks.html:
According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, carpenters:

  • Follow blueprints and building plans to meet clients’ needs
  • Install structures and fixtures, such as windows and molding
  • Measure, cut and shape wood, plastic and other materials
  • Build and install frameworks, including walls, floors and doorframes
  • Inspect and replace damaged framework or other structures and fixtures
  • Instruct and direct laborers and construction helpers

The work is indoors and outdoors, and it can mean cramped spaces and a lot of lifting, standing and kneeling. The most common injuries are strains from lifting and moving materials, along with falls, slips, trips and contact with objects or equipment. BLS lists these qualities as important: business skills, attention to detail, dexterity, interpersonal skills, math skills including basic trigonometry, physical strength, problem-solving and reading comprehension.

According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Occupational Outlook Handbook (page updated August 27, 2026), the median pay for carpenters was $60,580 a year, or $29.12 an hour, in May 2025. The lowest-paid 10 percent earned less than $40,410, and the highest-paid 10 percent earned more than $99,910. Median pay by industry: nonresidential building construction $63,780; building finishing contractors $60,880; residential building construction $60,600; foundation, structure and building exterior contractors $58,790.

There were 889,700 carpenter jobs in 2025, and employment is projected to grow 4 percent from 2025 to 2035, about as fast as the average for all occupations, with about 62,800 openings a year, mostly to replace workers who move to other jobs or retire. BLS expects population growth to drive new-home building, one of the largest employers of carpenters, while more use of modular and prefabricated parts built off-site tempers the growth. About a quarter of carpenters are self-employed. These figures are updated every year; check the handbook for the latest.

• High school: BLS says a high school diploma or the equivalent is typically required, and math and mechanical drawing classes help. Some vocational-technical schools offer associate’s degrees in carpentry.
  • On the job: most carpenters learn on the job or through an apprenticeship, starting with simple tasks like measuring and cutting wood and working up to reading blueprints and building structures.
  • Apprenticeships: unions and contractor associations sponsor apprenticeships that combine technical instruction with paid on-the-job training. A registered apprenticeship is a job: according to Apprenticeship.gov, apprentices earn a wage from day one, get raises as their skills grow, learn on the job and in the classroom with a mentor, and finish with a portable, nationally recognized credential. You can search for one with the Apprenticeship Finder.
  • Moving up: carpenters can advance to lead carpenter, first-line supervisor, independent contractor or general construction supervisor.

blocks.html:
OSHA’s Outreach Training Program teaches workers about job hazards, their rights, and how to file a complaint. The 10-hour construction course is mainly for entry-level workers, and the 30-hour course is for workers with some safety responsibility. Only OSHA-authorized trainers may teach these courses and issue the student course completion cards.

BLS says all carpenters must complete the OSHA 10-hour course. OSHA itself describes the program as voluntary: it says OSHA does not require completion of these courses, that the courses don’t fulfill the training required by OSHA’s standards, and that some states, cities and employers have made them mandatory. So check what your state and employer require. OSHA also warns about fraudulent courses, and says a course does not guarantee a job; it publishes a list of authorized trainers so you can check one.

BLS lists no license requirement for carpenters themselves: a driver’s license may be needed to reach job sites, and optional specialty certifications can open up more work. Running your own business is different: many states and cities license building contractors, so check your state’s rules. Construction and building inspectors usually need a license or certification: BLS says most states and localities require one.
