finder.name: Foundation cracks
finder.q: What does the crack look like?

opts.label: Thin, dry, and not changing
causes: Concrete shrinking as it cured and dried; some cracking is common in concrete and block foundations
Small, normal movement as the house settled
checks: Mark both ends with a pencil line and the date, and take a photo; check again every few months.
Keep water away: clean gutters, extend downspouts at least 4 feet, and keep soil sloped away from the wall.
opts.stop: If it grows, starts leaking, or one side shifts out of line with the other.
opts.pro: A foundation contractor can seal a crack that leaks; a structural engineer can tell you whether a changing crack matters.

opts.label: It leaks water after rain
causes: Rain or snowmelt soaking the soil next to the wall
Downspouts emptying right beside the foundation
Soil sloping toward the house
Clogged or missing drain tile
checks: Watch where the roof water goes in a rainstorm.
Extend downspouts at least 4 feet and slope the soil away (University of Minnesota Extension suggests at least 1 inch per foot for 6 feet).
Dry anything wet within 24 to 48 hours.
opts.stop: If water keeps coming in after the outside drainage is fixed.
opts.pro: A foundation or waterproofing contractor can seal the crack and check the drainage.

opts.label: Wide or growing, offset, or the wall bows or leans
causes: Soil or water pressure pushing on the wall
Settlement of the footing
Frost heave or drainage problems
checks: Photograph and measure it, with dates.
Note any doors or windows that have started to stick.
Don’t try to brace or repair it yourself.
opts.stop: Now: this is a structural question.
opts.pro: Have a structural engineer or experienced foundation contractor evaluate it. Structural repairs need a permit.

opts.label: Only in humid weather
causes: Wood swelling as it picks up moisture from humid air
High indoor humidity
Thick layers of paint on the edges
checks: Check indoor humidity; EPA suggests below 60 percent, ideally 30 to 50.
Look for loose hinge screws.
Wait for drier weather before trimming anything; the wood shrinks back.
opts.stop: If it gets worse year after year, or new cracks appear nearby.
opts.pro: A carpenter can adjust or plane the door once it’s dry.

opts.label: Suddenly, with new cracks in nearby walls
causes: The framing or foundation has moved
A sagging header over the opening
Water damage in the framing
checks: Check whether the door frame is still square: the gaps at top and sides should be even.
Look for new cracks at the corners of doors and windows, and mark them.
opts.stop: If the cracks keep growing or floors start to slope.
opts.pro: A structural engineer can find the cause before anything is adjusted.

finder.name: Water in the basement
finder.q: When does the water show up?

opts.label: After rain or snowmelt
causes: Roof water dumping beside the foundation
Soil sloping toward the house
Clogged gutters or downspouts
Window wells collecting water
High groundwater or failed drain tile
checks: Clean gutters and extend downspouts at least 4 feet from the wall.
Check that the soil slopes away from the house.
Look at window wells and the sump pump, if you have one: sump pumps can fail.
opts.stop: If water keeps coming in after the outside drainage is fixed.
opts.pro: A drainage or waterproofing contractor; dry the area within 24 to 48 hours to prevent mold.

opts.label: Damp walls in humid summer weather, even with no rain
causes: Warm, humid outdoor air condensing on the cool basement walls, often mistaken for a leak
Moisture from inside: a dryer that isn’t vented outdoors, showers, humidifiers
checks: Keep humid summer air out of the basement.
Make sure the dryer vents outdoors.
A dehumidifier can help with dampness and odor, but it doesn’t fix a water leak.
opts.stop: If you find standing water or mold growing.
opts.pro: An energy auditor or a basement moisture specialist.

opts.label: Standing water or flooding
causes: A broken or leaking pipe or water heater
A failed sump pump
Heavy storm runoff or high groundwater
checks: If it’s from a pipe, shut off the main water valve.
Dry everything you can within 24 to 48 hours; porous materials such as carpet may have to be thrown away if they get moldy.
opts.stop: Now: stop the water at the source if you can do it safely.
opts.pro: A plumber for leaks; for heavy water damage, a cleanup contractor experienced with mold.

opts.label: During or after rain
causes: Flashing at a chimney, vent pipe, skylight or roof-wall joint
Damaged or missing shingles
A missing kick-out flashing (stains on the wall below a roof-wall joint)
checks: Look at the roof from the ground.
From the attic, with a flashlight, look for wet wood or insulation and stains around penetrations.
Put a bucket under drips and move valuables.
opts.stop: Don’t climb onto the roof yourself.
opts.pro: A roofer, who works with fall protection.

opts.label: In winter, when there’s snow on the roof
causes: An ice dam backing water up under the shingles
Heat from the house leaking into the attic
checks: From the ground, look for thick ice along the eaves and icicles.
In the attic, look for gaps around lights, pipes and the hatch.
opts.stop: Don’t climb onto a snowy or icy roof.
opts.pro: A roofer for the leak; an insulation or weatherization contractor for the cause.

opts.label: It grows even when it hasn’t rained
causes: A plumbing leak above the ceiling
Condensation, such as a bathroom fan venting into the attic
An air-conditioning drain or duct sweating
checks: Note whether it’s below a bathroom or kitchen.
Check where the bathroom fan vents: it should go outdoors, not into the attic.
opts.stop: If the stain spreads quickly.
opts.pro: A plumber for leaks; an HVAC technician for ducts and drains.

opts.label: Thick ice along the eaves, big icicles
causes: Heat leaking into the attic warms the upper roof, snow melts, and the water refreezes at the cold eaves
Air leaks in the ceiling, thin insulation near the eaves
checks: Watch the ceilings and walls below for water stains.
In the attic, look for gaps around lights, pipes, chimneys and the hatch.
opts.stop: Don’t climb onto a snowy roof; University of Minnesota Extension suggests hiring professionals for work on the roof in winter.
opts.pro: A weatherization contractor can find the heat leaks with a blower door and an infrared camera, then air seal and insulate.

opts.label: Bounces, but it’s level
causes: Joists that are long for their depth (sag grows with the span to the fourth power)
Joists spaced wide apart
A heavy new load, such as a big aquarium or bookshelves
checks: From below, look at the joists for cracks, splits, or notches and holes cut by past plumbing or wiring work.
Look for signs of water damage.
opts.stop: If it starts to sag, crack or get worse.
opts.pro: A structural engineer can design stiffening.

opts.label: Visibly sags, or is getting worse
causes: A cut, cracked or overloaded joist or beam
Rot from a long-term leak
A bearing wall or post that was removed or moved
checks: Keep heavy loads off that area.
From below, look for cut joists, rot or a missing post.
opts.stop: Now: this is a structural question.
opts.pro: Have a structural engineer evaluate it. Structural repairs need a permit.

opts.label: A small spot, under about 10 square feet
causes: A leak, condensation or high humidity feeding it
checks: Find and fix the water source; cleaning alone lets mold come back.
Follow EPA’s cleanup guidance; don’t paint or caulk over mold.
Keep humidity below 60 percent, ideally 30 to 50.
opts.stop: If it comes back after cleaning, or you have health concerns.
opts.pro: Talk to a health professional if you have concerns before cleaning.

opts.label: A large area, or mold after flooding
causes: Heavy water damage
A long-term hidden leak
checks: Don’t run the heating and cooling system if you suspect it’s contaminated.
Porous materials such as ceiling tiles and carpet may have to be removed.
opts.stop: Now: big mold jobs need professional guidance.
opts.pro: EPA says to make sure a contractor has experience cleaning up mold.

opts.label: A musty smell, but no mold in sight
causes: Hidden mold: under carpet, behind walls, near roof or plumbing leaks
A damp basement or crawlspace
checks: Look around windows, under sinks, in the basement and under carpets.
Check the crawlspace for bare soil and damp wood.
opts.stop: If you find water damage inside walls.
opts.pro: A contractor experienced with mold can look inside walls.

opts.label: Near windows, doors or outlets
causes: Air leaks around frames, trim and outlets
Worn weatherstripping
checks: On a windy day, hold a lit incense stick near the edges and watch the smoke.
Caulk gaps and replace weatherstripping.
opts.stop: Before major air sealing, make sure fuel-burning appliances still get enough air.
opts.pro: An energy auditor can test the house with a blower door.

opts.label: A whole room is cold
causes: Missing or thin insulation in the walls, attic or floor
Air leaks at the rim joist or attic
A heating duct problem
checks: Check the attic insulation depth against ENERGY STAR’s table.
Feel for drafts at baseboards.
opts.stop: If you find vermiculite insulation in the attic, leave it alone and have it checked for asbestos.
opts.pro: An energy auditor; an HVAC technician for ducts.

opts.label: Small pops or hairline cracks at corners and joints
causes: Framing lumber shrinking as it dries and moving with the seasons
Normal movement in a newer house
checks: Patch them like any small hole.
If the house was built before 1978, work lead-safe when you sand old paint.
opts.stop: If cracks grow, or doors start sticking.
opts.pro: A drywall finisher for many repairs at once.

opts.label: Long diagonal cracks from door or window corners that keep growing
causes: Movement in the framing or the foundation
A sagging header
checks: Mark the ends with the date and watch them.
Check nearby doors for sticking.
opts.stop: If they keep growing.
opts.pro: A structural engineer can find the cause before the cracks are patched.

opts.label: Outside, on siding, trim, fascia or soffits
causes: Water getting into or behind the wood: leaks, overflowing gutters, missing flashing or caulk
Water getting into the roof edge (bubbled paint on fascia or soffits is a warning sign)
checks: Look for the water source: gutters, flashing, cracked caulk.
If the house was built before 1978, assume the paint may contain lead.
opts.stop: Don’t dry-scrape or sand paint on a pre-1978 house without lead-safe practices.
opts.pro: A painter certified under EPA’s lead renovation rule for pre-1978 homes; a roofer or carpenter for the water source.

opts.label: Inside, in a bathroom or kitchen
causes: Moisture from showers and cooking
An exhaust fan that’s missing, too weak or not used
checks: Run the bathroom fan during and after showers, and the range hood while cooking.
Make sure the fan vents outdoors.
opts.stop: If mold grows under the paint.
opts.pro: An electrician or contractor to add or upgrade a fan.

ladder.title: First jobs
ladder.sub: Basic tools, no permits, and nothing structural.

jobs.t: Find a stud and hang a picture
Patch a small hole in drywall
Find and test your main water shutoff
Test smoke and CO alarms
Clean gutters you can reach safely; extend downspouts
Keep soil and mulch sloped away from the foundation
Test your home for radon
Find drafts with an incense stick and caulk small gaps

ladder.title: Next steps
ladder.sub: More tools, more care, and an experienced helper the first time.

jobs.t: Weatherstrip doors and windows
Paint a room (lead-safe in pre-1978 homes)
Replace baseboard or door casing
Adjust a sticking door: hinges and strike plate
Patch a larger drywall hole with a patch
Run a dehumidifier and track humidity
Set up and use an extension ladder by OSHA’s rules

ladder.title: Intermediate jobs
ladder.sub: Check with the building department first; some of these need a permit.

jobs.t: Frame a non-load-bearing partition wall
Hang, tape and finish drywall in a room
Install a pre-hung interior door
Lay a floating floor or tile
Air seal the attic, then add insulation (watch for vermiculite)
Build a small shed (permit rules vary)

ladder.title: Leave these to licensed pros and engineers
ladder.sub: They need a permit, training, special equipment, a license or certification, or an engineer’s design.

jobs.t: Removing or changing load-bearing walls, beams, headers, posts or trusses
Foundation repairs, underpinning, and cracks that keep growing
Roof work at height (OSHA requires fall protection at 6 feet for workers)
Digging trenches 5 feet or deeper (OSHA requires protective systems)
Paid work that disturbs paint in pre-1978 homes (EPA certification)
Anything that may disturb asbestos (trained, accredited professionals)
Mold over about 10 square feet, or after heavy water damage
Gas piping, electrical panels and service, and refrigerant (see those courses)
